content: The following recommendations and updates are essential for improving HIV patient monitoring and care delivery systems: 1. Integration of Monitoring Tools: Patient monitoring tools should incorporate demographic, clinical, laboratory, adherence, and psychosocial criteria to assess and document eligibility for Differentiated Service Delivery (DSD) models. These tools should also track the specific DSD elements provided, such as antiretroviral therapy (ART) refills, clinical monitoring, adherence support, and the location of service delivery (e.g., community, clinic, pharmacy, or laboratory). 2. Electronic Medical Records (EMRs): EMRs should capture key data such as ART drug pick-up dates, the quantity of ART dispensed, and other services provided (e.g., psychosocial support, adherence counseling, or laboratory testing). 3. Adaptability of DSD Models: As DSD models evolve, patient monitoring tools and EMR systems must remain flexible and adaptable. Facilities relying on paper records should revise ART registers or create new ones specific to DSD models to monitor uptake and outcomes effectively. 4. Time-Organized Data: Information related to DSD services should be organized chronologically (e.g., monthly) from the initiation of DSD services. Key elements to record include the date of DSD eligibility assessment, classification of eligibility, start date of DSD, type of DSD model, ART pick-up dates, and clinical visit dates. 5. Reasons for Exclusion from DSD: Reasons for exclusion from DSD models, such as pregnancy, opportunistic infections, increased viral load, healthcare worker concerns, adverse drug reactions, or patient preference, should be documented. Exclusions may be temporary, requiring reassessment within a specified timeframe. 6. Community ART Services: Monitoring tools for community-based ART services need to be developed and implemented. These tools should be simple, user-friendly, and capable of tracking DSD ART services and client follow-up. Data confidentiality and security are critical, especially in community settings. 7. Data Flow and Quality: Data from community-delivered services must be transmitted to health facilities in real-time for transcription into the HIV patient monitoring system. Both paper-based and electronic reports should be securely stored. 8. National Implementation in Mozambique: Mozambique has implemented a national DSD guideline, scaling up 3-month and 6-month ART drug dispensing and introducing one-stop service delivery models. The country uses a standardized paper-based tool (master card) for HIV patient monitoring, with codes assigned to various DSD models. Data from these tools are entered into EMRs in high-volume facilities, covering over 80% of ART patients. 9. Performance Reviews: Mozambique conducted its first DSD data performance review in 2021 to assess health facility coverage, client coverage, service quality, retention, and viral load suppression. Quantitative and qualitative data were collected from sampled facilities, and findings were used to improve service delivery. 10. Data Confidentiality for Key Populations: Data related to behaviors that may be stigmatized or criminalized (e.g., same-sex sexual activity, sex work, or drug use) should not be included in ART registers or reported to national data units. Clinical records should only include information that is clinically relevant and kept secure to protect client confidentiality. 11. Gender Data Collection: In settings where being transgender or gender-diverse is stigmatized, facility records may include only male and female categories for gender. In other settings, gender identity and sex assigned at birth can be recorded to improve patient management and data disaggregation. 12. WHO Minimum Dataset: The 2022 WHO minimum dataset for HIV testing and treatment includes updates to reflect the latest recommendations. These updates cover ART regimens, eligibility for DSD, rapid ART initiation, and monitoring of disengagement from care. Laboratory and clinical data elements have also been revised to align with current guidelines. 13. Program Monitoring for Key Populations: Safeguards must be in place to protect client identities. 14. Referral Systems: Programs like Malawi’s EpiC initiative use referral tickets to track clients referred from key population programs to public health facilities. 15. Quality Improvement: National quality improvement guidelines, such as Mozambique’s Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles, are used to address areas of poor performance. Indicators such as DSD uptake, quality of care, and viral load suppression are assessed to develop action plans for improvement.
